t: #3893 Maximum Team Size with Overlapping Intervals — Center Interval Counting
o: A valid team needs one member (the center) whose interval overlaps every other member's; members need not overlap each other. So the answer is the maximum, over all intervals i, of the number of intervals overlapping interval i (including i itself). Overlap means sharing at least one point: [s1,e1] and [s2,e2] overlap iff s2 <= e1 and s1 <= e2. Example 1: [1,4] overlaps both others, answer 3. Example 2: no interval overlaps any other, answer 1. With n up to 1e5 we cannot compare all pairs; instead sort all start points and all end points and binary search: intervals NOT overlapping [s,e] are exactly those with start > e or end < s.
k: The answer equals max over centers i of |{j : start_j <= end_i and end_j >= start_i}|.
Sort the starts and ends separately; count non-overlapping intervals via binary search (starts beyond e, ends before s).
Every interval overlaps itself, so the answer is at least 1.

a.i: Sort the array of start times and the array of end times independently. For a center interval [s,e], the count of intervals with start <= e is bisect_right(starts, e), and the count with end < s is bisect_left(ends, s). Their difference counts intervals satisfying both conditions, i.e., overlapping the center.
s: Copy and sort startTime into S and endTime into E.
For each i, compute cnt = bisect_right(S, endTime[i]) - bisect_left(E, startTime[i]).
Return the maximum cnt over all i.
a.t: O(n log n) — sorting dominates; each of the n queries is two binary searches.
a.sp: O(n) — sorted copies of the endpoint arrays.

a.i: Sort events (+1 at each start, -1 at each end, ends processed before starts at the same coordinate so touching intervals count as overlapping). The maximum prefix sum gives the largest number of simultaneously live intervals — which equals the maximum overlap clique around some point. Note this answers a slightly stronger question (common intersection point); when a common point exists it matches the center formulation, and it serves as an intuitive alternative worth discussing in interviews.
s: Create events (time, type) with ends processed before starts at equal times.
Sweep in time order maintaining a running counter of active intervals.
Track the maximum counter value and return it (at least 1).

w: In an interview, lead with the binary-search-on-sorted-endpoints approach since it exactly matches the problem definition; mention the sweep as intuition for why dense regions yield big teams. Pitfalls: off-by-one at shared endpoints (touching intervals DO overlap, hence bisect_right / bisect_left choices), and forgetting the self-overlap guaranteeing a minimum answer of 1. Follow-up: what if ANY member must interact with every other (clique instead of star) — that becomes a much harder structure.
